_about: Concepts: working notes for the NYC OSPO executive summary. Public version .

sections.title: About this draft
sections.body_md:
- Bullet points for the NYC OSPO executive summary, to be written up as prose
- Two models:
  - Haddad's report for how an OSPO is structured, staffed and phased (Haddad 2022)
  - the CMS office for a U.S. government doing it, with tools New York could adopt (DeCausemaker 2024a; Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c)
- Draws first on Final notes; Munich, Paris, the European Commission and the UN are short supporting examples
- Citations link to their entries and show their status:
  - plain underline = Final notes
  - amber = Draft Notes, not yet verified; each section header counts them
  - flags clear on their own when an entry moves to Final notes
- [Input needed: …] marks anything the bibliography can't support

sections.title: Summary
sections.body_md:
- City agencies already use open source, but no one in the City's central technology agency is responsible for it
  - no full picture of what's in use
  - no one checking licenses are met and dependencies kept current
  - no one helping the next agency reuse what another built
- In Haddad's maturity model the City is at the ad hoc stage: agencies consistently use open source internally (Haddad 2022)
- A small, permanent OSPO within OTI would move the City to the next stage: compliant licensing, educating developers, and an inventory of the open source the City runs (Haddad 2022)
- Structure: Haddad's virtual OSPO, a head of open source and a small core team working with staff across agencies who give part of their time (Haddad 2022)
  - New York already has a version of that network: the Open Data Coordinators every agency must name (NYC Open Data Law 2012)
- Starts as a strategic consumer of open source, not a publisher of it (Haddad 2022)
- Much of the work is already automated by public-domain CMS tools:
  - a five-tier repository maturity model that could be copied exactly for use within OTI (DeCausemaker 2024a)
  - a repository scaffolder that generates the files and checks each tier needs (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c)
  - a metrics dashboard that tracks every repository's health (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a)
  - code.json, the metadata file federal agencies now use to inventory their code (SHARE IT Act 2024)
- Four outcomes (DeCausemaker 2024a):
  - saving time and money
  - accountability for contractors' performance
  - less duplicate work
  - lower security and continuity risks
- [Input needed: the ask.] Which decision, by whom: an OTI directive, a mayoral executive order, or a Council local law. Versions of this executive summary may be altered depending on who we are presenting to.
- [Input needed: one New York number,] Cases or figures of how open source methodology could save money, reduce duplicate work, or improve a current tool.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body_md:
- New York has written "open by default" into local law once, for data: Local Law 11 of 2012 (NYC Open Data Law 2012)
  - every agency's public data on one portal
  - a technical standards manual the City keeps on GitHub
  - amendments added archiving, data dictionaries, deadlines for public requests, and an Open Data Coordinator in every agency
- It covers data, not source code. Nothing requires the City to inventory or share the code it pays for (NYC Open Data Law 2012)
  - that's the gap an OSPO would fill
- The federal government closed the gap for its own agencies with the SHARE IT Act of 2024 (SHARE IT Act 2024):
  - custom code stored where other agencies can reach it
  - its metadata published
  - rights secured to share code bought from contractors
  - turned code sharing from a policy without enforcement into a requirement with deadlines and reporting
  - doesn't apply to New York City
- The work Haddad lists for this stage has no owner in City government today (Haddad 2022):
  - reviewing open source activity for license compliance
  - an inventory that shows unmet license obligations and security vulnerabilities
  - criteria for which open source to adopt
- CMS framed the same problem around duplicate work, security, continuity and value for public money (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- A mandate needs people: in 2024 the team carrying out the Open Data Law was six people, and about half of 872 data sets flagged for automation weren't automated (NYC Open Data Law 2012)
- [Input needed: the City's GitHub organizations] and how many repositories each holds
- [Input needed: two or three named examples] of open source the City runs
- [Input needed: one documented case] of the same software bought or built twice
- [Input needed: whether any City code built with federal funds carries federal sharing obligations]

sections.title: Two models: Haddad and CMS
sections.body_md:
### Haddad: the framework

- The most complete account of how OSPOs are structured, what they do and what gets in their way (Haddad 2022)
- Drawn mainly from corporate OSPOs, which assume different structures and bigger budgets than a city can expect (Haddad 2022)
- New York would take the framework, not the scale:
  - the maturity stages
  - the virtual structure
  - the roles to cover
  - the four strategy stages: consumer, participant, contributor, leader

### CMS: the practice

- The first OSPO in a U.S. federal agency (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- Its lead's DEF CON deck sets out how it works: a functional statement, a five-tier maturity model, release checklists, a metrics dashboard and automated repository checks (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- Makes the case for supporting the outside projects the agency depends on (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- Nearly every claim links to a public repository or page that can be checked (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- Model for a deck of our own (DeCausemaker 2024a):
  - frames the work around serving the public, saving taxpayers money and strengthening government
  - takes on the common myths about open source one by one
- Its tools do much of the heavy lifting this proposal asks of an OSPO (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c)
- Public domain, so the City could copy and adapt them freely (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a)

### How CMS started and held up

- Stood up in 2023, launched publicly January 2024 (Miller 2024)
- Team of about five (Queram 2025)
- 2025: parent agency renamed and lost a third of its staff; the OSPO's tools survived because they were public (Fortune 2025)
- June 2026: Federal Register charter, with at least 20% of new custom code to be released as open source (CMS 2026)

### Its limits

- Ran on a one-paragraph statement for almost three years
- Staff served fixed terms, which its lead named as a constraint, along with pressure to show results within a year (CHAOSS 2024)
- [Input needed: It may be better for New York to write that mandate down earlier and make the positions permanent?}

sections.title: Structure, team and founding document
sections.body_md:
### A virtual OSPO

- A head of open source (here a small team) working with people from other teams who each give a share of their time (Haddad 2022)
- Usually no dedicated budget; spending would come through OTI (Haddad 2022)
- Sits within OTI, close to the engineers who build and run City systems

### Agency liaisons

- Since 2017 every agency has had to name an Open Data Coordinator (NYC Open Data Law 2012)
- An open source liaison in each agency could work the same way

### Roles to cover

- Haddad's list of roles; in a team of two or three, several would be combined (Haddad 2022)

| Role | What it covers | In New York |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head of the OSPO | Deep open source knowledge, strong technical background, licensing and best practice, ties to the OSPO community | The primary hire. Also the main evangelist, with champions already inside OTI |
| Senior engineer | Technical work, including the tooling | A full-stack generalist, like those hired to PITCrews |
| Technical evangelist | Public work and technical documentation that build support | Combined with the head |
| Compliance engineer | License obligations | Combined with the senior engineer |
| Legal counsel | Licensing and contract questions | General counsel, not in-house |

### Permanent posts

- CMS's lead named fixed terms as a constraint (CHAOSS 2024)
- Munich made two of its four launch posts permanent (Stadt München 2023a)

### The founding document

- Would name the office, its host, its five functions, its permanent posts, its agency liaisons and a yearly public report
- [Input needed: the instrument:] an OTI directive, a mayoral executive order or a Council local law. The Open Data Law was a local law (NYC Open Data Law 2012)
- [Input needed: civil service titles and salary bands] for two or three posts
- [Input needed: which agencies name liaisons first]

sections.title: Strategy: start as a consumer
sections.body_md:
- Haddad's four strategy stages: consumer, participant, contributor, leader (Haddad 2022)
- First phase: a consumer, using open source strategically rather than producing it
- Consumer-stage work (Haddad 2022):

### 1. Review all open source activity, including license compliance

- Where open source is used across agencies, and whether its license terms are met

### 2. A classification scheme for what to adopt

- Explicit criteria (Haddad 2022):
  - features available
  - maturity of the source code
  - size and makeup of the developer community
- Judge each option on need, cost and risk, using total cost of ownership over the system's life (DoW CIO 2026)
- Outside evaluation frameworks exist, such as QSOS and OSMM (DoW CIO 2026)
- CMS's early criteria are a worked example: existing products, maturity, costs and risks, licensing (Fletcher, DeCausemaker and Colón Viera 2022)
- Federal rules treat open source as commercial software, so it gets equal consideration with proprietary products in market research (DoW CIO 2026)
  - [Input needed: whether City procurement rules treat it the same way]

### 3. Inventory open source with a software bill of materials (SBOM)

- Lists the components in each system, to find unmet license obligations and security vulnerabilities (Haddad 2022)
- code.json gives every repository a standard record the inventory could build on (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c; SHARE IT Act 2024)

### 4. Automated workflow software for evaluating open source use

- Lets a small team cover many repositories (Haddad 2022):
  - metrics pulled from the GitHub API and git logs
  - automated security checks
  - repository scaffolding
  - CI harnesses that run checks every time code is deployed
- Scales across repositories without adding staff
- The CMS tools already do most of it (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c; Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a)

### Phasing

- Start with non-critical systems, and avoid ties to proprietary formats (DoW CIO 2026)

### Communicate it

- Explain the strategy throughout OTI, with education for staff (Haddad 2022)
- Encourage teams to find and adopt good open source and be open about the tools they use
- Follow project mailing lists, attend conferences, join open source foundations, host events, invite others to present (Haddad 2022)

### Share inside first

- Innersource: share code between teams before sharing it publicly (Haddad 2022)
- For New York: agencies share with each other first
- Some public-sector offices skip this and build in the open from the start (Linåker et al. 2026)

### Education

- A core OSPO function and key to an office that lasts (Haddad 2022)
- May not be in scope for the earliest stage, but critical to long-term success and reputation

sections.title: What the office would do
sections.body_md:
### 1. Manage: one place and one standard for City code

- Every agency gets access to the City's designated code platform, with one set of rules
- Every repository placed in a tier of the CMS maturity model, which could be copied exactly for use within OTI (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- New repositories start from the CMS scaffolder's templates (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c)

### 2. Find: know what the City runs

- Review all open source activity and take the SBOM inventory (Haddad 2022)
- Identify the staff who look after each project; make sure they have tools and support

### 3. Catalog: make it findable

- Turn the inventory into a catalog of City code and the open source the City depends on
- Agencies check what exists before they buy or build
- A code.json file in every repository could be its basis (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c)
- Same format federal agencies now publish; Databook or govoss could publish a City code inventory in it (SHARE IT Act 2024)

### 4. Support: keep it maintained and secure

- Answer staff questions
- Apply the classification scheme before a team adopts a tool (Haddad 2022)
- Every tool the City runs has a support and sustainment plan; community help alone isn't enough (DoW CIO 2026)
  - support for open source "is often sold separately" (DoW CIO 2026)
- Automated checks on every repository (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c; TODO Group n.d.)
- A clear, secure route to release City code, at the City's discretion
- The mechanism that keeps the City compliant with the licenses it uses (Haddad 2022)

### 5. Expand: reuse and, later, contribute

- Adopt proven tools from elsewhere once City code is managed to these standards
- In time, contribute back: the participant stage (Haddad 2022)

### What it would not do

- Immediately replace existing systems or direct agency purchasing; instead it gives agencies one place to ask whether a proven alternative already exists
- Publish sensitive databases

sections.title: The toolkit
sections.body_md:
- First five rows are from Final notes; the rest are from Draft Notes and are flagged
- CMS tools are public domain (CC0): adopting them costs staff time, not licenses

| Tool | Where it lives | What it does | What New York would adapt |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Repository maturity model | [ospo-guide: Maturity Models](https://dsacms.github.io/ospo-guide/outbound/maturity-models/) | Five tiers of openness, each with its own requirements (DeCausemaker 2024a) | Nothing. Could be copied exactly for use within OTI |
| repo-scaffolder | [github.com/DSACMS/repo-scaffolder](https://github.com/DSACMS/repo-scaffolder) | Tier script; templates for each tier's files; a release checklist per tier; Repolinter configs; GitHub Actions that push template updates; a code.json generator (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c) | Built for federal requirements, so parts need adapting to City rules. Depends on Repolinter |
| Repolinter | [github.com/todogroup/repolinter](https://github.com/todogroup/repolinter) | Checks each repository for a license, README, contributing guide, code of conduct and changelog, on its own, before a commit, or in CI (TODO Group n.d.) | Nothing to build: the scaffolder ships a ruleset for each tier and runs it through CMS's own GitHub Action, [DSACMS/repolinter-action](https://github.com/DSACMS/repolinter-action). That action runs New Relic's fork of Repolinter (v0.9.2), and the original was archived February 6, 2026, so the checking engine gets no updates. Worth watching, not blocking (checked in both repositories, November 11, 2026) |
| Metrics site | [github.com/DSACMS/metrics](https://github.com/DSACMS/metrics) · [live](https://dsacms.github.io/metrics/) | Weekly GitHub Action pulls from the GitHub API and Augur (CHAOSS) into charts of repository health (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a) | Customized to New York's metrics. Augur needs its own server and database |
| OpenSSF Scorecard | [github.com/ossf/scorecard](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard) | From the Open Source Security Foundation, which sets cybersecurity standards for open source. Scores a project on 12+ security metrics. CMS uses it alongside its metrics site (Miller 2024) | Run on every City repository and on the outside projects the City depends on |
| code.json | [SHARE IT Act guide](https://dsacms.github.io/share-it-act-lp/) | Standard metadata file per repository, used for federal code inventories (SHARE IT Act 2024) | Could work as is |
| Open source FAQ | [DoD-OSS-FAQ on GitHub](https://risacher.github.io/DoD-OSS-FAQ/) | Answers the usual objections; kept on GitHub, where anyone can suggest changes by pull request (DoW CIO 2026) | A City version kept the same way, next to the Open Data Technical Standards Manual, answering City questions |
| Outbound checklists | [ospo-guide](https://dsacms.github.io/ospo-guide/outbound/outbound-checklists/) | Four tiers of release checklist with technical, business and security sign-off (CMS OSPO n.d.-b) | City sign-off roles |
| Exemption criteria | [ospo-guide](https://dsacms.github.io/ospo-guide/outbound/exemption-criteria/) | When code stays closed (CMS OSPO n.d.-d) | City categories, with counsel |
| Inbound Review Checklist | [ospo-guide](https://dsacms.github.io/ospo-guide/inbound/inbound-review-checklist/) | Sign-offs before a team adopts an open source tool (CMS OSPO n.d.-f) | A working form of Haddad's classification scheme |
| codejson-index-generator | [github.com/DSACMS/codejson-index-generator](https://github.com/DSACMS/codejson-index-generator) | Collects every repository's code.json into one index (DSACMS n.d.-c) | Run across every City GitHub organization |
| Apache Project Maturity Model | [Apache Community Development](https://community.apache.org/apache-way/apache-project-maturity-model.html) | Judges a project's community health (Apache Software Foundation n.d.) | Pairs with the CMS tiers |

### Infrastructure

- Open source-friendly IT infrastructure is critical; an environment too strict for open knowledge sharing and contributions could be a large blocker (Haddad 2022)
- Broader approval to communicate with outside participants and contribute to projects reduces friction (Haddad 2022)
- [Input needed: what OTI's environment allows today]

sections.title: Measuring results
sections.body_md:
- Metrics should be tracked. Choosing them is "one of the more difficult tasks for an OSPO," and the metrics product teams use don't apply to open source (Haddad 2022)
- Choose them with the office's champions: CMS's lead consulted the CIO and CISO on which metrics to prioritize (CHAOSS 2024)
- First step: learn who the champions are in OTI and City Hall, and what they need to see
- Candidate measures:
  - repositories released (Miller 2024)
  - pull requests and contributions (Miller 2024; Haddad 2022)
  - time for issues to be resolved (Miller 2024)
  - number of contributors (Miller 2024)
  - code reuse, such as a tool picked up by a second agency (Miller 2024)
  - security risks mitigated:
    - OpenSSF Scorecard results: 12+ security metrics per project, as CMS uses (Miller 2024)
    - libyears, how far behind a project's dependencies are (DeCausemaker 2024b)
  - costs reduced (DeCausemaker 2024b; CMS OSPO n.d.-i)
  - our own proposals, with no public source yet:
    - how regularly updates ship
    - how long contributors stay
    - people hired and events attended
- Most can come from the CMS metrics site, which tracks "contributor activity, issue resolution times, code complexity and dependency health"; hiring, events, risks mitigated and costs reduced tracked by hand (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a)
- The metrics site is a good starting place, customized to New York's needs (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a)
- CMS sorts measures into maturity, cost and burden, and uses COCOMO to put a dollar figure on the effort in its code (DeCausemaker 2024b)
- A yearly public report, modeled on the Open Data Law's annual compliance plan, published each September 15 (NYC Open Data Law 2012)
- [Input needed: who the office's champions are,] and what they need to see
- [Input needed: a baseline,] ideally from the first inventory

sections.title: Guardrails
sections.body_md:
### Open source doesn't mean publishing everything

- The CMS deck takes on the risks and myths of open source one by one (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- First myth CMS had to clear up: that open source means releasing data or personal information (Miller 2024)
- Sharing between agencies is "not the same thing as public release as OSS" (DoW CIO 2026)
  - inventory and sharing between agencies come first; public release is a separate decision

### Security

- "Merely hiding source code does not counter attacks" (DoW CIO 2026)
- Security depends on review and timely fixes; open and proprietary software both need case-by-case evaluation (DoW CIO 2026)

### Compliance and review

- The OSPO is the mechanism that tracks the City's license obligations (Haddad 2022)
- Each maturity tier has its own release checklist (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c)
- Every repository checked automatically for the files and policies its tier requires (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c; TODO Group n.d.)

### Some code stays closed

- SHARE IT Act model (SHARE IT Act 2024):
  - classified and national security code exempt automatically
  - a CIO can exempt code for export-control or security laws, or an identifiable privacy risk
  - each exemption reported every year
- A City policy could follow the same pattern

### Ownership and licensing

- Federal contractors usually keep the copyright to software built with government funding; the government can release code it holds unlimited rights to (DoW CIO 2026)
- CMS owns the code that it pays contractors to produce (Miller 2024)
  - [Input needed: what rights the City gets in its software contracts.]
- Federal work can't be copyrighted, so open is the federal default; City work can be (Fletcher, DeCausemaker and Colón Viera 2022)
  - [Input needed: a default license for City code, with counsel]

sections.title: Cost
sections.body_md:
- The method is free: CMS's tools are public domain (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a; Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c)
- Virtual model: usually no dedicated budget; spending comes through the host organization (Haddad 2022)
- For New York:
  - two or three permanent posts in OTI
  - part of each agency liaison's time
  - hosting for the metrics site, and for Augur if needed (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a)
- Supporting example: Munich funded its office with €500,000 in start-up money and two permanent posts (Stadt München 2023a)
- [Input needed: salaries for two or three posts at OTI's rates,] and hosting costs

sections.title: Where it could go
sections.body_md:
- The participant stage is an eventual necessity; the stages beyond it would raise New York's standing in technology governance. The City isn't there yet (Haddad 2022)
- In that stage the City would (Haddad 2022):
  - file bug reports and contribute fixes to the projects it depends on
  - improve or extend their functionality, and implement new features
  - take security measures to improve the City's products
  - contribute source code from its own development, to show good faith and earn standing
- Federal precedent: DoD policy authorizes employees to contribute to open source projects as part of their official duties (DoW CIO 2026)
- Ties with organizations that lend resources and legitimacy, especially once the City contributes regularly (Haddad 2022):
  - the TODO Group and the Apache Software Foundation
  - the Software Freedom Law Center and the Open Invention Network, for legal questions
- CMS makes the same case for supporting the outside projects an agency depends on (DeCausemaker 2024a)

sections.title: Supporting examples
sections.body_md:
- All from Draft Notes, so flagged
- **Munich:**
  - created by a council decision naming its host, a team of four with two permanent posts, €500,000 in start-up funding, and four jobs (Stadt München 2023a)
  - 110 public repositories with more than 90 staff contributing, four months after opening (Stadt München 2024)
- **Paris:**
  - formed around a platform the city already ran; Lutece supports more than 200 city services (Paris n.d.)
  - one officer alongside a 15-person engineering team (Bareille 2023)
- **European Commission:**
  - shared code platform, code.europa.eu: 737 repositories by December 2024 (EC OSPO 2024)
  - innersource raised the share of internal code open to other departments from about 10% to more than 30% (OSOR 2026 (meetup slides))
- **United Nations:**
  - surveyed its organizations before writing rules; all used open source, none had a governance framework (Tridgell 2026)
  - framework lets each organization adopt practices in stages (Open Source United 2024)
  - community meets every June at UN Headquarters in Manhattan (UN 2025)

sections.title: Outside input needed
sections.body_md:
### From the City or OTI

- The City's GitHub organizations and repository counts
- Two or three named examples of open source the City runs
- One documented case of the same software bought or built twice
- What OTI's IT environment allows for outside collaboration and contributions
- Whether City procurement rules treat open source as commercial software
- What rights the City gets in its software contracts
- Civil service titles and salary bands for two or three posts
- Hosting costs for the metrics site and Augur
- Who the office's champions are, and what they need to see

### Decisions for you

- The founding instrument: an OTI directive, an executive order or a local law
- A default license for City code, with counsel
- Which agencies name liaisons first
- Whether education and training are in scope for the first stage

### Research to finish

- Low priority: whether New Relic's Repolinter fork, which CMS's linting action runs, is still maintained
- Whether Augur can be skipped by running the metrics site on GitHub API data alone
- Whether City code built with federal funds carries federal sharing obligations
- Verify the Draft Notes entries this draft still cites (the amber citations), or cut what depends on them
